sources: Texas Parks and Wildlife, Introducing Mammals: Skunks: each of the two glands holds about a tablespoon of musk, enough for five or six shots; a full refill takes several days; can fire right, left, front and back without turning around; targets within ten to twelve feet usually in range; warns by arching its back, raising its tail and stamping its front feet, and may rear on its front legs as if doing a handstand to spray over its head; a direct hit in the face can cause painful but temporary blindness; insects and grubs are at least half its diet; great horned owls and coyotes occasionally kill skunks; https://tpwd.texas.gov/publications/nonpwdpubs/introducing_mammals/skunks

Illinois Department of Natural Resources, Wildlife Illinois, Striped Skunk: size of a small house cat; can accurately direct its musk up to 10 feet, some reaching nearly 20 feet; stamps its front feet and raises its tail as a warning; the musk is butyl mercaptan, a strong sulfur odor; can carry rabies; odor-removal mix of 3% hydrogen peroxide, baking soda and liquid soap; https://wildlifeillinois.org/identify-wildlife/striped-skunk/

National Geographic Kids, Skunk: great horned owls are a main predator, and scientists think their weak sense of smell makes the spray useless against them; https://kids.nationalgeographic.com/animals/mammals/skunk/

beats.say: A skunk can hit you in the face from ten feet away.
The striped skunk. About the size of a house cat.
Under its tail, two glands, each holding about a tablespoon of stinky musk.
That's enough for ten or twelve shots.
And it can aim left, right, front, or back, without even turning around.
The smell is a sulfur chemical, called butyl mercaptan.
